/about.title: About PortTrip — The DIY Cruise Port Planning Authority
/about.desc: PortTrip is built by cruisers who got tired of overpriced ship excursions. We publish real transport routes, exact prices, and port day plans built around your all-aboard time. Here's who we are and how we work.
/about.h1: We built this because ship excursions cost too much.
/about.html:
About PortTrip

We built this because ship excursions cost too much.

The average ship excursion to Rome from Civitavecchia costs €120–€180 per person. The same day, independently, costs €35–€50. We've done both. The train wins most of the time.

PortTrip exists to give every cruiser what the ship doesn't: exact bus numbers, real walking times, actual prices, and the confidence that they'll be back before the gangway lifts.

What PortTrip actually does

Research every port independently

We don't publish transport routes we haven't verified. For each port, we check bus frequencies, taxi prices, walking distances from the terminal, and whether the route is actually feasible in 6–8 hours. Prices are updated seasonally.

Build around your all-aboard time, not theirs

Every itinerary we build works backwards from your ship's all-aboard time with a 90-minute safety buffer built in. We don't optimize for "seeing more" — we optimize for "getting back." Missed ships ruin cruises.

Tell you when DIY is NOT the right call

Some ports are not worth going alone. Tender ports in bad weather, ports with no reliable transport, ports where the ship excursion is genuinely cheaper — we flag all of these. We'd rather you trust us than take a risk.

Track what excursions actually cost

We monitor what cruise lines charge for their own excursions and compare it to realistic DIY costs. When the gap narrows, we say so. When the DIY route is risky, we say so too.

Our honest view on ship excursions

Ship excursions aren't always a scam. Some are genuinely excellent — particularly for remote ports, tender-heavy landings, and anywhere security queues are unpredictable. If you're on a tight itinerary with elderly travellers or young kids, the convenience is worth paying for.

But for major Mediterranean cities — Barcelona, Rome (via Civitavecchia), Dubrovnik, Athens (via Piraeus), Kotor, Lisbon — the DIY route is usually cheaper, often faster, and frequently better. You eat where locals eat. You skip group dynamics. You move at your own pace.

The problem isn't that ship excursions are always wrong. The problem is that cruisers are rarely given honest information to make the comparison. PortTrip changes that.

PortTrip is built by Elke, in Maastricht. I started it after watching cruise passengers pay for a coach tour to a city they could have reached on a €3 bus — and after seeing how stressful the return to the ship is when you're doing it alone. PortTrip plans the day around your all-aboard time so you can go on your own with a clear plan. If something in a guide is wrong, email hello@porttrip.com and I'll fix it.

/methodology.html:
PortTrip Methodology

How PortTrip scores cruise ports

Every PortTrip recommendation is built on three proprietary frameworks: the DIY Savings Index, the Ship-Safe Timing Buffer, and the DIY Difficulty Score. Here's exactly how each one works.

Last updated: May 2025 · Data covers 50+ cruise ports globally.

Cruise Port Independence Index · 2026 Edition

Reproducible DIY score methodology

The score is a weighted average. Each input is 0–100; weights total 100%. Missing cost data produces limited_data and no score.

20% · transport Reliability

Reliability and clarity of transport between terminal and primary sights.

10% · distance

Penalty for long terminal-to-destination transfers.

10% · transfer Simplicity

Fewer required transfers score higher.

15% · tender Friction

Dock ports score higher; tender and cable-car queues reduce the score.

15% · time Sensitivity

How forgiving the return journey is when delays occur.

10% · walkability

Ease of reaching useful sights on foot or with simple local transport.

10% · cost Advantage

Savings percentage versus the comparable ship excursion.

10% · return Buffer Feasibility

Ability to retain the recommended return buffer in a normal full port day.

Methodology v1.0 · Published 2026-08-19 · Last updated 2026-08-19

Framework 1

DIY Savings Index

The DIY Savings Index measures how much cheaper the independent alternative is compared to the median ship excursion price for the same destination. It's expressed as a percentage and a euro amount.

Formula

DSI = ((Ship Excursion Price − DIY Cost) / Ship Excursion Price) × 100

What goes into "Ship Excursion Price"

We take the median price of the top 3 most popular ship excursions to the same destination (typically: city highlights tour, historical site visit, and beach/leisure option). We check 4–6 major cruise lines per port annually. Prices are sourced directly from cruise line booking systems, not third-party aggregators.

What goes into "DIY Cost"

DIY Cost includes: return transport from port to city centre (bus/train/taxi), entry fees to main attractions, and a mid-range lunch. It excludes shopping. Where a taxi is the only realistic option, we use local taxi rates — not tourist estimates. DIY Costs are updated seasonally (April and October).

Framework 2

Ship-Safe Timing Buffer

The Ship-Safe Timing Buffer (SSTB) is our most conservative calculation. It determines the latest possible departure time from any attraction that still guarantees you're back at the gangway before all-aboard closes.

Formula

SSTB = All-Aboard Time − (Transit Time × 1.25) − 30 min gangway queue − 15 min contingency

Why ×1.25? Real transit takes longer than Google Maps suggests. Missed buses, passport queues, port security, and the occasional wrong platform all add up. We apply a 25% buffer to every transit time — then add another 45 minutes of fixed contingency on top.

Why 30 minutes for gangway queue? On busy port days (especially at Dubrovnik, Kotor, and Mykonos), returning passengers queue. We've seen 25-minute gangway waits on tender days. We build this in by default.

What happens in the planner? Every AI-generated itinerary enforces the SSTB. The app shows a live countdown to your "leave now" time. If you add a stop that pushes past the buffer, the app flags it.

⚠ Tender ports add extra buffer

For tender ports (Santorini, Kotor, some Dubrovnik itineraries), we add an additional 45 minutes to account for tender queues at both ends. Missing a tender is the same as missing the ship.

Framework 3

DIY Difficulty Score

The DIY Difficulty Score (1–10) rates how hard it is to navigate a port independently. A score of 1 means anyone can do it with Google Maps. A score of 9+ means we'd recommend a ship excursion.

Scoring dimensions (each 0–2 points)

Transport clarity

How clear and reliable is the public transport from terminal to city?

Language barrier

How much does not speaking the local language impede navigation?

Walking difficulty

Does reaching the main sights require significant climbing or distance?

Time pressure

How tight is the itinerary relative to all-aboard time?

Crowd/queue risk

Do peak season crowds significantly reduce available time?

1–3

Easy

Solo-friendly, reliable public transport

4–6

Moderate

Doable with preparation

7–10

Ship excursion may be worth it

Ports we say you should NOT DIY

PortTrip actively flags ports where the DIY route is genuinely risky or poor value. This is not a hedge — it's our honest assessment based on difficulty score, timing constraints, and reported experiences.

Santorini

Cable car queues can hit 90 minutes in summer. Tender delays add another 45. On a 6-hour port call, DIY to the caldera is genuinely tight. We flag this.

Mykonos (tender)

Tender queues on cruise days can be 30–40 minutes. The old town is walkable once ashore, but the return trip is where people miss ships.

Kotor (tender)

The old town is beautiful and easy to walk. But tender days at peak season create 45-minute return waits. Don't cut it close.

/editorial-policy.title: Editorial Policy | PortTrip
/editorial-policy.desc: How PortTrip researches, verifies, dates and corrects cruise-port recommendations.
/editorial-policy.html:
Editorial policy

PortTrip separates verified facts, estimates and recommendations. We name the basis for costs and transport guidance, show confidence, and recommend the ship excursion when independent travel is not the responsible default.

Verification

Priority port costs, transport routes, tender constraints and return buffers are checked against named public operators, port authorities or dated price samples.

Dates

Last-verified dates change only after a substantive review, never automatically on deployment.

Commercial independence

Affiliate or purchase opportunities do not determine the verdict. Missing data is labelled limited_data.

Corrections

Material corrections are documented and propagated to the decision dataset and affected pages.

/corrections.desc: How to report a factual correction to PortTrip cruise-port data and recommendations.
/corrections.html:
Corrections

Found an outdated fare, changed transport route, terminal instruction or recommendation that needs review? Email info@porttrip.com with the port, affected page, source link and date observed.

What happens next

  1. We verify the report against an authoritative source.
  2. We update the source dataset and every affected visible page.
  3. We change the last-verified date only after review.
  4. Material recommendation changes are recorded here.

No material corrections recorded for the 2026 Edition as of 19 August 2026.

Read the editorial policy

/privacy.title: Privacy policy | PortTrip
/privacy.desc: How PortTrip collects, uses and protects your data when you plan cruise port days, buy a plan or use the leave-by tools, and how to exercise your rights.
/privacy.html:
Legal

Privacy Policy

Last updated: 12 October 2026

We built PortTrip to help cruisers plan smarter. We take your privacy seriously and keep this policy as clear and jargon-free as possible. If you have questions, email us at info@porttrip.com.

1. Who We Are

PortTrip is an AI-powered cruise port planning platform. We help passengers plan their time in port — including itineraries, transport, budgets, and booking recommendations. References to "PortTrip", "we", "us", or "our" in this policy refer to the PortTrip service and its operators.

2. What Data We Collect

Account Information

  • Email address (used to create and manage your account)
  • Display name (if provided)
  • Account role and subscription tier

Itinerary & Planning Data

  • Cruise details you enter (ship name, ports, dates, all-aboard times)
  • Day plans and port itineraries you create
  • Stops, preferences (travel mode, group type, budget), and notes
  • Expenses you log within the app

Usage & Analytics

  • Pages and features you interact with
  • Events such as plan generation, ticket link clicks, and itinerary exports
  • Device type, browser, and approximate location (country-level)
  • Session duration and navigation patterns

Crew (tours organised by passengers)

If you propose or join a Crew tour, we store your display name, email address, the sailing and the tour you signed up for. Your display name and email address are shared with the tour's Organiser; an Organiser's email address is shared with the tour's Members. We use this data only to run Crew and to send the emails that belong to it (for example, when someone joins or a tour is cancelled). The legal basis is the performance of the service you asked for. We delete Crew data no later than 90 days after the sailing ends. Organisers and Members may use each other's details only to coordinate that tour (see section 9 of our Terms).

Payment Information

If you subscribe to a paid plan, payment is processed by Stripe. We do not store your card number or payment credentials. We only receive confirmation of payment and your subscription status.

3. How We Use Your Data

  • To generate and personalise AI-powered itineraries for your port visits
  • To save and sync your plans across devices
  • To show relevant port guides, tips, and booking recommendations
  • To manage your account and subscription
  • To improve the product based on aggregate usage patterns
  • To send transactional emails (e.g. login links, subscription receipts)
  • To comply with legal obligations

We do not sell your personal data. We do not use your data for advertising targeting by third parties.

4. Cookies and Tracking

We use a small number of cookies and similar technologies to keep you logged in, remember your preferences, and understand how the product is used.

Types of cookies we use:

  • Session cookies — required for login and authentication
  • Preference cookies — remember your settings (e.g. view mode, language)
  • Analytics cookies — understand feature usage and page performance (aggregated, not sold)

You can disable non-essential cookies in your browser settings. This may affect some features of the app.

5. Third-Party Services

PortTrip integrates with several third-party services to deliver its features:

  • Google Maps — for interactive port maps and location data (governed by Google's Privacy Policy)
  • OpenAI — AI-generated itinerary content is processed via OpenAI's API (no personal data is sent, only planning context)

By accessing or using PortTrip (the "Service"), you confirm that you are at least 13 years old and agree to these Terms of Service ("Terms"). If you are using the Service on behalf of an organisation, you represent that you have authority to bind that organisation to these Terms.

  • Track timing, transport, and budgets for port excursions
  • Access port guides, travel tips, and community insights

  • Manage multiple cruises and port days in one place

The Service is provided on a subscription basis. Some features are available on a free tier; others require a paid Cruise Pass or Pro subscription.

Important: Itineraries are advisory only.

All itineraries, transport times, route suggestions, and cost estimates generated by PortTrip are provided for planning guidance only. They are not a guarantee of real-world conditions.

Specifically, you acknowledge and agree that:

  • Transport estimates (walking times, taxi durations, transit routes) are approximations and may differ from actual conditions

  • AI-generated recommendations are based on historical data and general knowledge — not live, verified information
  • You are solely responsible for verifying all practical details before your port visit

You are responsible for returning to your cruise ship on time.

PortTrip provides planning tools and time buffers as guidance. However, PortTrip is not responsible for missed ships, missed all-aboard times, additional travel costs, or any consequences arising from a passenger not returning to their vessel on time.

Always allow more time than you think you need. All-aboard times are strictly enforced by cruise lines and ships do not wait. If in doubt, err on the side of caution and return to the port earlier.

6. Subscriptions and Payments

  • The Cruise Pass is a one-time payment; Pro is billed yearly in advance

You can ask for a full refund within 30 days of your purchase. Contact us using the details in section 16 and we will refund the full amount you paid. You do not have to give a reason.

We strive to recommend only reputable providers, but always verify booking details directly with the operator.

9. Crew: Tours Organised by Passengers

9.1 What Crew is. Crew lets passengers on the same sailing propose, join and coordinate shore tours with each other. Every tour on Crew is proposed and run by a passenger (the "Organiser"). The passengers who join are "Members".

9.2 PortTrip's role. PortTrip only provides the space where tours are listed and coordinated. PortTrip:

  • is not the organiser, operator, seller or agent of any Crew tour
  • is not a party to any agreement between Organisers, Members and tour providers
  • does not take payment for Crew tours and does not earn a commission on them
  • does not check, select, vet or endorse any tour, Organiser, Member or provider

9.3 Who may organise. You may propose a tour only if you are a passenger booked on that sailing, you are at least 18 years old, and you act as a private individual. Tour operators, guides, drivers and other businesses may not propose tours, recruit passengers or advertise on Crew. You may not use Crew to sell anything.

9.4 Prices and payment. The price shown on a tour is the Organiser's estimate per person. It is not an offer from PortTrip. You pay the provider, or settle with the Organiser, directly. PortTrip has no part in that payment. Do not send money to anyone you have not met. The provider's own terms decide refunds, cancellation and any dispute about price.

9.5 Organiser responsibilities. As an Organiser, you are responsible for what your listing says, including the meeting point, meeting time, price estimate and back-by time. You must describe the tour honestly, tell Members promptly if the plan changes, and cancel the tour on Crew if it will not go ahead. Choosing a provider is your decision and your responsibility.

9.6 Your own responsibility. Joining a Crew tour is your own decision. Before you join, you are responsible for judging whether the tour, the provider and the plan suit you, including licences, insurance, safety, accessibility and local requirements such as visas or the documents you must carry ashore. Treat a Crew tour as you would any arrangement made with fellow travellers you have not met before.

Section 4 applies in full to Crew tours. Each passenger is personally responsible for being back on board before all-aboard time, whatever the Organiser, other Members or the provider do. If the group is running late, leave the group and make your own way back. Ships do not wait for independent tours.

When you organise a tour, your email address is shared with your Members. Use these details only to coordinate that tour. Do not add anyone to mailing lists, pass their details on, or contact anyone after they have left or cancelled. Our Privacy Policy explains how PortTrip handles this data.

9.9 Content rules. You must not post false, misleading or unlawful content; advertising, links or payment requests; other people's personal data; or content that harasses, discriminates against or endangers others.

We may remove a tour, end a signup or restrict a user's access to Crew if we reasonably believe these Terms or the law have been broken. When we do, we will tell the affected user what we removed and why, unless the law prevents us. That user can reply to ask us to review the decision.

PortTrip is not liable for the acts or omissions of Organisers, Members or providers; the quality, safety, legality or cancellation of any Crew tour; any payment made for a Crew tour; or any missed all-aboard time or departure. Section 11 applies to Crew. Nothing in these Terms limits or excludes liability for intent or gross negligence, or any liability that cannot be limited or excluded under mandatory law.

PortTrip is an AI-powered cruise port day planner. It generates personalized, time-accurate itineraries for cruise passengers who want to explore ports independently — without paying for expensive ship excursions.

PortTrip data indicates that cruise passengers who plan independently save an average of €60–€100 per person per port. PortTrip provides the exact transport directions, attraction sequencing, and safety timing that makes independent port exploration reliable — not just cheaper.

Using PortTrip, a passenger enters their port city, all-aboard time, group type, and travel style. The AI generates a complete day plan — including which bus or train to take from the terminal (with exact stop names and costs), which attractions to prioritise, and a precise must-leave time that includes a 90-minute safety buffer.

PortTrip analysis shows that the majority of "missed ship" incidents occur because passengers underestimate return journey time or don't account for tender port delays. PortTrip's timing engine accounts for both, and alerts users when they need to start heading back.

How to return to your cruise ship on time

A 6-step system used by independent cruisers to guarantee they make it back before all-aboard — at every port, in every season.

1

Know your all-aboard time — not departure time

All-aboard time is posted at your cabin and the gangway. Departure is typically 30 minutes after all-aboard. You must be back before all-aboard.

2

Calculate your buffer (90 minutes minimum)

Work backwards: All-Aboard − 90 min = latest you should arrive at the port terminal. For tender ports, subtract another 30–40 minutes.

3

Know your return transport before you leave

Before disembarking: check taxi cost to port, nearest train/bus stop, and last reliable departure time back. Save the port address offline.

4

Set a physical departure alarm from your furthest point

Not from the ship. From wherever you plan to be furthest from the port. Build travel time + buffer into this alarm.

5

Have the taxi fallback route pre-researched

6

Return early if anything feels uncertain

Weather delays, transport strikes, medical emergencies. If you feel the timeline is tight — leave now. Sights can be seen next time. The ship waits for no one.

Common questions

What time should I return to the cruise ship?

Arrive at the port terminal (not just in port town) at least 90 minutes before all-aboard. For tender ports, add 30–45 minutes for the tender queue. Factor in travel time from your furthest point.

What if I am running late for the cruise ship?

Call the ship (number in your cruise card or app) immediately. Take a taxi directly to the port — do not wait for public transport. If you miss the ship, you will need to self-fund travel to the next port.

Does the cruise ship wait if you are late?

No. Cruise ships operate on strict port scheduling and will depart at the published time. All-aboard time is the absolute deadline. Ships regularly leave with passengers still on the dock.

How to Never Miss Your Cruise Ship

The exact 5-step system: must-leave time calculation, 90-minute buffer rule, tender port protocol, and what to do when you think you're running late.

Quick Answer

To never miss your cruise ship: subtract 90 minutes from all-aboard time to get your "must-leave" city time. For tender ports (Santorini), use 120 minutes. Then subtract your return journey time on top. At Santorini with a 17:00 all-aboard, be at the tender pier by 15:00 — the queue alone can take 75 minutes.

Why ships actually get missed — and it's not bad luck

Missing a cruise ship doesn't happen to reckless or disorganised passengers. It happens to thoughtful, experienced travellers who made one specific miscalculation. The most common: treating the all-aboard time as "be approaching the ship at 17:00." It isn't. The gangway closes at 17:00 — you need to already be through security, card scanned, and physically on board before that moment. Planning for arrival at 16:55 leaves no margin for the security queue, the gangway crowd, or the 3-minute walk from the terminal entrance.

The second most common cause: the cascade effect. A 20-minute late start compounds through the day. By 15:00, the passenger who started 20 minutes late is now 60–80 minutes behind plan — facing a choice between cutting everything or accepting real risk. Time-stamped itineraries with explicit departure times at every stop make this cascade visible before it becomes critical.

The 5-step system — in order

1

Calculate your "must-leave" time — not the all-aboard time

Your all-aboard time is the moment the gangway closes. It is not your target return time. After accounting for security, boarding queue, and gangway processing, your personal target should be 30 minutes before all-aboard — already on board, not arriving.

From there, subtract your return journey time from the city. Barcelona: 25–35 min. Dubrovnik: 15 min. Rome from Civitavecchia: 90 min by train. Naples: 20 min walk. The result is your "must-leave" time. Write it down. Set an alarm 15 minutes before it. Treat it as non-negotiable.

💡 Rule: your target is to be on board 30 min before all-aboard, not arriving at the terminal.

2

Apply the 90-minute buffer rule (120 for tender ports)

The 90-minute buffer covers the return journey (15–90 min by port type), securing transport (5–20 min on a busy afternoon), terminal security and check-in (15–30 min), and a 15-min contingency. Add those up: 60–110 min under normal conditions.

For tender ports — Santorini, some Norwegian fjord stops — the buffer is 120 minutes minimum. Return tender queues in peak season at Santorini regularly run 45–75 minutes. This is documented consistently across passenger reports on busy summer days.

💡 75 min — documented max tender return queue at Santorini in peak season (July–August).

3

Research your return transport the night before — not at the pier

The afternoon is the wrong time to figure out how to get back. The evening before, confirm: which transport you'll take back, exactly where you board it, how long it takes, and the last viable departure time.

💡 10 minutes of transport research the night before is worth 30 minutes of margin the next day.

4

Pre-identify your "cut stop" before the day starts

Before you disembark, decide which stop you will skip if the day runs behind. Not after things go wrong — before, with a clear head. Your cut stop should be the furthest or lowest-priority attraction.

Write it down: "If we're 30+ minutes behind at 13:30, we skip the castle and head directly to the bus stop." This decision, made in advance, means you cut calmly rather than agonising under pressure at 15:45.

💡 Pilots call this "identify your divert airport before you need it." Port days work exactly the same way.

5

Call the ship immediately if you think you might be late

Every cruise ship has a passenger services contact number — save it before you disembark. If you're at 16:20 in a city with a 17:00 all-aboard, call immediately. Don't wait and hope. Ships have occasionally held gangways for nearby passengers who communicated early. They never wait for passengers who don't.

The buffer you need varies significantly by port type. Walk-off ports give you nearly all your time in quality — the return to the ship is 5 minutes. Train-transfer ports like Rome from Civitavecchia consume 2.5–3 hours in Zone 1 and Zone 3 combined. Know which type you're at before the day starts.

Santorini: The most dangerous port for timing

Santorini is a tender port — you reach shore on small boats. The return tender queue in peak season regularly runs 45–75 minutes when multiple ships are anchored. This is not an edge case; it happens consistently on busy summer days.

Rule: for a 17:00 all-aboard, be at the tender pier by 15:00. Not 15:30.

Additional factor: cable car up takes 20–45 min queue in peak season. Solution: walk the 580 steps instead (25 min, no queue). Use buses for Oia return — don't rely on afternoon taxis (scarce).

Save the passenger services number before you disembark. Calling early (even if you end up making it back fine) is always better than not calling.

2

3

Every cruise line has one. Call the ship, call your travel insurance, and ask what the next port is. It's recoverable — but it's expensive and stressful.

Emergency guidance · what to do now

What happens if you miss your cruise ship?

The ship will sail without you.

This is the hard reality. Cruise ships operate on strict port schedules with berth reservations and pilotage windows. They will not wait for independent travellers beyond the all-aboard time. If you are already late, call the ship immediately — the next steps are below.

If this is happening right now

1

Call the ship's emergency number — now

The number is on your cruise card and in the cruise line app. If the ship is still in port, a call may hold departure by minutes. Do not wait.

2

Take a taxi directly to the port

3

Go to the port agent office if the ship has left

Every cruise line has a port agent in every major port. They are your contact point for reaching the next destination. Ask port authority staff for their location.

4

Book travel to the next port immediately

Check your cruise itinerary for the next port. Book flights or fast transport immediately — delay makes everything more expensive. Use Google Flights or a travel agent at the port.

5

Contact your travel insurance

File a missed departure claim as soon as possible. Keep receipts for everything — accommodation, transport, meals. Some policies cover these costs.

What it costs to rejoin the ship

Emergency flight to next port

One or two nights accommodation

Ground transfers at both ends

Missed boarding fee (some lines)

Total typical cost

How to never let this happen again

The 90-minute buffer rule: Plan to be at the port terminal 90 minutes before all-aboard. Not in the city. Not on the bus. At the terminal.

For tender ports, add 45 minutes: Santorini and Mykonos queues run 35–50 minutes each way in peak season. This is not optional buffer — it is required timing.

Know the taxi fallback price: Before leaving the ship each morning, know the taxi cost and time to the port. This is your emergency route if everything else fails.

Set a departure alarm from your furthest point: With transport time and buffer already calculated. Not a reminder to "start heading back" — a specific alarm for the moment to leave.

What happens if you miss your cruise ship?

The ship sails without you. You are responsible for your own travel to the next port at your own cost. Contact the cruise line port agent immediately — they have a local representative in every port who can advise on reaching the next destination. You will need to self-fund flights, accommodation, and transfers.

Will the cruise ship wait for you if you are late?

No — unless you are on a ship-organised excursion that has been delayed (in which case the ship will wait for the group). The ship will not wait for independent travellers. All-aboard time is the hard deadline.

Who do you contact if you miss your cruise ship?

Call the ship's emergency number (on your cruise card) immediately. Contact the cruise line's port agent (they have an office in every major cruise port). If you cannot reach either, go to the port authority office — they can contact the ship on your behalf before it leaves.

Yes. And it happens every season.

You booked a local tour operator (not through the cruise line) that is delayed

You lost track of time at an attraction

Public transport was delayed

Ship-organised excursion buses are officially delayed

The ship will wait only for passengers on ship-organised excursions that have experienced an official delay — a delayed excursion bus, for example. For all independent travellers, the all-aboard time is absolute. There are no exceptions.

Return timing · direct answer

How late can you return to a cruise ship?

You must be on board before all-aboard time. Not arrival at the port — on board.

The all-aboard time posted on your cabin door and at the gangway is the absolute deadline. The gangway closes at this time. The ship typically departs 15–30 minutes later, but being on the dock when the gangway closes means you have missed the ship.

All-aboard time vs departure time — the difference matters

All-aboard time

The time you must be physically on the ship. The gangway closes at this time. This is your deadline.

Departure time

When the ship leaves the dock. Usually 15–30 min after all-aboard. Being on the dock at this time means you're already too late.

What happens at different timing scenarios

90+ min before all-aboard

Safe

You are in the port area with a full buffer. Standard return. No risk.

45 min before all-aboard

OK but no margin

You should be at or near the terminal. Any unexpected delay — closed road, no taxi — could cause a problem.

20 min before all-aboard

High risk

You should already be at the terminal. If you are still in the city, take a taxi immediately. No public transport.

At all-aboard time

Miss the ship

The gangway is closing now. You need to be at the gangway — not arriving at the terminal, not parking. If you are not physically at the gangway, you may miss the ship.

The 90-minute rule: why it works

Planning to be at the port terminal 90 minutes before all-aboard covers every realistic delay scenario: transport disruptions (20–30 min), terminal queues (10–15 min), security screening (5–10 min), and walking to the gangway (5–10 min). That leaves 20–30 minutes of true safety margin.

At tender ports, the tender queue adds 35–50 minutes to your return. Add 45 minutes to the standard buffer — plan to be at the tender pier 135 minutes before all-aboard.

What is the difference between all-aboard time and departure time?

All-aboard time is when you must be physically on the ship — the gangway closes at this time. Departure time is when the ship leaves the dock, usually 15–30 minutes later. You must meet the all-aboard time, not the departure time.

How early should you be back at the ship?

PortTrip recommends arriving at the port terminal 90 minutes before all-aboard. This gives you time for any unexpected delays. At tender ports, add 45 minutes for the tender queue. This is the rule that eliminates virtually all missed-ship risk.

Can you run to the ship if you are running late?

Sometimes — if you are close to the port and the gangway is still open. Call the ship immediately if you are running late. They can sometimes keep the gangway open for a few extra minutes. But do not count on it. Take a taxi if you are cutting it close.

/leave-by-widget.h1: Tell your readers when to head back to the ship.
/leave-by-widget.html:
Tell your readers when to head back to the ship.

A free widget for cruise blogs. Your reader sets their all-aboard time and gets a leave-by time for every part of the port, from 172 checked port guides. One paste. No iframe, no cookies.

Optional. Readers can change it. Leave empty to use the guide's usual time.

Look

Paste this where the widget should go

<div class="porttrip-leaveby" data-port="kotor"><a href="https://porttrip.com/ports/kotor">Kotor cruise port guide</a> by PortTrip</div> <script async src="https://porttrip.com/embed/leave-by.js"></script>

Keep the link in the snippet. It shows inside the widget and it is how this stays free.

What your readers see

Kotor cruise port guide by PortTrip

Shown here on a white page with a serif font, like a typical blog. The widget takes your site's font.

Questions bloggers ask

Does it slow my page down?
It is one 28 KB script, loaded with async, so your page renders first. No iframe, no fonts, no cookies.
Where does the data come from?
The same checked port guides as porttrip.com. Each leave-by time counts back from your reader's all-aboard, using the travel times and buffers in the guide. Every guide lists its official sources and the month it was last checked.
Will it look wrong on my site?
It draws inside its own sealed box, so your theme cannot break it, and it picks up your site’s font. Choose light, dark, or match the reader’s setting.
What does it cost?
Nothing. The only condition is that the link to the port guide stays in the snippet.
Which platforms does it work on?
Anything that accepts HTML: WordPress (Custom HTML block), Squarespace (Code block), Wix (Embed code), Ghost (HTML card), Blogger, and hand-built sites.

How the score works

  • Getting to town, up to 4 points. Walk to the centre in 20 minutes or less: 4. Longer walk: 3. Walk or short ride, or tender: 2. Transport needed: 1.
  • Return safety, up to 4 points. Low risk of missing the ship on a normal day on your own: 4. Medium (shuttles, buses, queues): 2. High (the usual day out depends on trains, long transfers or tender queues with known gaps): 0.
  • Time in town, up to 2 points. How early you must leave the centre to be back on board in time, counted back from all-aboard. 75 minutes or less: 2. Up to 105 minutes: 1. More: 0.

Inputs come from each port's PortTrip guide, which lists its sources: port authorities, transport operators and official attraction sites, checked in October 2026. Berths change from call to call; the score reflects the usual berth for large ships. No port, cruise line or tour operator pays to be included or ranked.

Common questions

What is the PortTrip Cruise Port Index?

A ranking of 172 cruise ports by how easy they are to do on your own, without a ship excursion. Each port gets a score out of 10 for getting to town, return safety and time in town, based on PortTrip guides checked against official sources in October 2026.

Which cruise port is easiest to do on your own?

The top of the index is ports where the ship docks in walking distance of the centre, the return carries little risk and you can stay in town until about 75 minutes before all-aboard. See the table for the current order.

Which cruise ports are hardest without an excursion?

Ports where the town is far away (Rome from Civitavecchia, Florence from Livorno), where you tender in and queue to get back (Santorini), or where the usual day out depends on trains with long gaps.

How is the score calculated?

Getting to town is worth up to 4 points, return safety up to 4 and time in town up to 2. The full method is on this page. No port pays to be listed.

Can I use this data?

Yes. You can cite the index and its scores with a link to porttrip.com/cruise-port-index.

/cruise-port-rules.h1: Cruise port rules, caps and fees for 2026 and 2027
/cruise-port-rules.html:
Checked October 2026

Cruise port rules, caps and fees for 2026 and 2027

Ports are charging cruise passengers more and letting fewer of them in at once. This page lists the 36 rules that change a port day: access fees, passenger taxes, daily caps, bans and terminal moves. 30 are in force now. Every entry says who pays, from when, its current status and where the information comes from, with official sources first. Where we could not confirm something, the entry says so.

By Elke, founder of PortTrip. Spotted a change? Email hello@porttrip.com and we will check it.

36 of 36 shown

Venice

Italy · Fee

In force

Day visitors aged 14+ entering the historic centre between 08:30 and 16:00 on 60 set days must pay an access fee and carry a QR code; cruise passengers only passing through the Stazione Marittima terminal do not pay.

Amount
€5 if booked 4+ days ahead; €10 if booked within the last days before the visit
Who pays
Passenger, paid directly on the city portal (not added by the cruise line). MSC says its own shore excursions include the fee.
From
3 April–26 July 2026 (fee days: Apr 3–6, 10–12, 17–19, 24–30; May 1–3, 8–10, 15–17, 22–24, 29–31; Jun 1–7, 12–14, 19–21, 26–28; Jul 3–5, 10–12, 17–19, 24–26)
Status
in force (2026 season); 2027 dates not yet published

Sources

  • Calendar: when will you need to pay a fee to visit Venice in 2026 (The Local Italy)
  • Ticket di ingresso a Venezia 2026 confermato fino a 10 euro per 60 giornate (Qualitytravel.it)
  • Destination fees and local charges (MSC Cruises)
Venice cruise port guide

Venice

Italy · Ban

In force

Ships over 25,000 gross tonnes (and others exceeding length, air-draught or fuel-sulphur limits) are banned from the San Marco Basin, San Marco Canal and Giudecca Canal; in 2026 large ships still use Fusina, Marghera and Chioggia rather than the historic centre.

Who pays
Cruise line (operational restriction)
From
1 August 2021 (decree-law 103/2021); unchanged for 2026
Status
in force

Sources

  • Larger cruise ships banned from Venetian Lagoon starting August (Seatrade Cruise News)
  • Al via la stagione crocieristica di Venezia nel 2026 (Shipping Italy)
Venice cruise port guide

Greek ports (other than Santorini and Mykonos)

Greece · Fee

In force

Every cruise passenger visiting a Greek port pays a per-port fee that varies by season.

Amount
€5 (1 Jun–30 Sep); €3 (1 Apr–31 May and October); €1 (1 Nov–31 Mar), per person per port
Who pays
Passenger, all ages; lines add it to the onboard account (some only if you go ashore) and remit it to the Greek tax authority. AIDA will collect it directly from guests on 2027 cruises booked from 1 August 2026.
From
21 July 2025
Status
in force

Sources

  • Destination fees and local charges (MSC Cruises)
  • Greece introduces cruise passenger tax to address overtourism (Eurofast)
  • AIDA Cruises to pass Greek taxes to guests (Cruise Industry News)

Santorini

Greece · Fee

In force

Santorini carries the highest tier of the Greek cruise passenger fee.

Amount
€20 (1 Jun–30 Sep); €12 (1 Apr–31 May and October); €4 (1 Nov–31 Mar), per person per call
Who pays
Passenger, all ages; usually charged to the onboard account by the cruise line
From
21 July 2025
Status
in force

Sources

  • Destination fees and local charges (MSC Cruises)
  • Greece's new sustainable cruise tax officially begins (TravelPulse)

Mykonos

Greece · Fee

In force

Mykonos carries the same top-tier Greek cruise passenger fee as Santorini.

Amount
€20 (1 Jun–30 Sep); €12 (1 Apr–31 May and October); €4 (1 Nov–31 Mar), per person per call
Who pays
Passenger, all ages; usually charged to the onboard account by the cruise line
From
21 July 2025
Status
in force

Sources

  • Destination fees and local charges (MSC Cruises)
  • Greece introduces cruise passenger tax to address overtourism (Eurofast)

Santorini

Greece · Visitor cap

In force

Santorini limits cruise visitors to about 8,000 a day, down from peaks of 16,000–17,000.

Amount
8,000 cruise passengers per day
Who pays
Cruise lines (arrival scheduling)
From
2025 season onwards (as reported)
Status
in force as reported by trade press; no official decree or legal text found

Sources

  • Santorini caps cruise crowds as Europe tightens controls (Luxury Travel Advisor, 30 Jun 2026)
  • Greece to increase port fees and limit cruise ships at most popular islands (Maritime Executive, Sep 2024)
Santorini cruise port guide

Santorini

Greece · Terminal change

In force

Only 30% of tendered cruise passengers may land at Athinios each day; the other 70% must land at the old port (Ormos Fira), reached by cable car or 600 steps.

Who pays
Cruise lines (fines or suspension for non-compliance)
From
June 2026
Status
in force; legality questioned by the Naxos prosecutor

Sources

  • Santorini implements new cruise tender limits (Cruise Industry News)
Santorini cruise port guide

Dubrovnik

Croatia · Visitor cap

In force

Dubrovnik allows at most two large cruise ships a day, each staying at least eight hours, and caps cruise visitors in the city at 4,000 at any one time; ships with 500 or fewer passengers are exempt from some rules.

Amount
2 ships per day; 4,000 cruise visitors at once
Who pays
Cruise lines (berth allocation by the Port Authority)
From
2026 berthing regulations (published 29 July 2024); two-ship limit in place since 2019
Status
in force

Sources

  • 2026 Cruise berthing regulations – Dubrovnik Port Authority (EU Transition Pathways for Tourism)
  • Dubrovnik announces moves to stop overtourism in the city (Croatia Week, Sep 2025)
Dubrovnik cruise port guide

Barcelona

Spain · Tax

In force

Cruise passengers in port for under 12 hours pay the city tourist-tax surcharge plus the Catalan regional tax; the city plans to raise its part from €8 to €24.

Amount
Now: up to €8 municipal + €6 regional per person per day. Planned: €24 municipal + €6 regional = up to €30
Who pays
Passenger, collected through the cruise line
From
Increase expected in 2027 (needs end-of-year fiscal ordinance); timing not fixed
Status
current rate in force; increase approved by city council, not yet in force

Sources

  • Barcelona approves 24 euro tax for cruise passengers (Cruise Industry News, Jul 2026)
  • Acord PSC-ERC-Comuns per encarir fins a 30 euros la taxa turística als creueristes (betevé, Jun 2026)
Barcelona cruise port guide

Barcelona

Spain · Terminal change

Announced

The port is cutting cruise terminals from seven to five: terminals A, B and C will be demolished and replaced by one new terminal for 7,000 passengers that prioritises home-port and smaller ships.

Who pays
Cruise lines
From
Works 2026–2030 (first step: close the south-wharf terminal and demolish terminal C)
Status
announced (agreement signed July 2025)

Sources

  • Protocol with the port to improve the management of cruise ships (Barcelona City Council)
  • 5 bans that will affect popular cruise ports in 2026 (Islands)
Barcelona cruise port guide

Valencia

Spain · Terminal change

In force

The Dique del Este and Muelle de Levante berths are closed to cruise ships for the 2026 season because of building work, with priority for home-port calls.

Who pays
Cruise lines
From
2026 season
Status
in force; reports of a ban on ships over 5,000 passengers are unconfirmed by the port

Sources

  • Procedimiento confirmación escalas cruceros 2026 (Valenciaport)
  • 5 bans that will affect popular cruise ports in 2026 (Islands)
Valencia cruise port guide

Palma de Mallorca

Spain · Visitor cap

Announced

Palma allows three cruise ships a day, only one with more than 5,000 passengers, and cuts the summer daily average from 8,500 to 7,500 berths.

Amount
3 ships/day; 7,500 berths/day average June–September 2027–2029 (8,500 rest of year)
Who pays
Cruise lines (voluntary agreement with the Balearic government, Palma council and CLIA)
From
Renewed 2026; summer cut applies 2027–2029; agreement runs five years
Status
announced (agreement signed)

Sources

  • Palma to reduce cruise ship berths in summer from 2027 (Travel Weekly UK)
  • Renewed Palma cruise agreement tightens passenger limits (CruiseMapper, Jun 2026)
Palma de Mallorca cruise port guide

Nice and Villefranche-sur-Mer

France · Ban

Not in force

A mayoral decree capping ships at 450 passengers in Nice and 2,500 in Villefranche was suspended by the Nice administrative court, which ruled the mayor lacked the power.

Amount
Would have been: 450 passengers (Nice), 2,500 (Villefranche)
Who pays
Cruise lines
From
Decree of 9 July 2025; suspended 13 July 2025
Status
suspended by court; not in force

Sources

  • French court suspends cruise ship ban in Nice and Villefranche-sur-Mer (Seatrade Cruise News)
  • Mayor of Nice shouts 'get lost' at Royal Caribbean ship (Marine Insight)

Cannes

France · Visitor cap

In force

Cannes caps cruise landings at 6,000 passengers a day and keeps ships carrying more than 1,000 passengers out of the harbour (they must anchor and tender).

Amount
6,000 passengers per day
Who pays
Cruise lines
From
1 January 2026
Status
in force (voted by city council 2025)

Sources

  • Cannes introduces cruise ship limits (TravelMole, Jul 2025)
  • Cannes limits daily cruise ship passengers to 6,000 (CruiseMapper)
  • 5 bans that will affect popular cruise ports in 2026 (Islands)

Marseille

France · Emission rule

In force

Shore power went live at the cruise terminal, able to plug in three very large ships at once; connection is encouraged but no formal obligation or cap was found.

Who pays
Cruise lines
From
11 April 2026
Status
in force (infrastructure); no mandate confirmed

Sources

  • Marseille eyes record 2.8M passengers as shore power goes live (Seatrade Cruise News, Sep 2026)
Marseille cruise port guide

Amsterdam

Netherlands · Visitor cap

In force

Amsterdam caps sea-cruise calls at the central Veemkade terminal at 100 a year (down from about 190), will require shore power from 2027 and aims to move the terminal out of the centre by 2035.

Amount
100 calls per year
Who pays
Cruise lines
From
2026 (cap); 2027 (shore power); 2035 (terminal out of centre)
Status
cap in force; relocation or full ban by 2035 still to be decided

Sources

  • Amsterdam wil aantal cruiseschepen halveren en passagiersterminal verplaatsen (NOS)
  • Amsterdam considers banning cruise ships altogether (DutchNews, Jan 2026)

Amsterdam

Netherlands · Tax

In force

Cruise passengers pay Amsterdam's day-tourist tax for each day their ship is in the city.

Amount
€15 per person per day (municipal ordinance); one news report says €22 from 2026, not confirmed
Who pays
Passenger, collected via the cruise line
From
Current ordinance version valid from 22 November 2025
Status
in force

Sources

  • Verordening Dagtoeristenbelasting 2019, Amsterdam (overheid.nl)
  • Amsterdam plafonne les croisières à 100 navires en 2026 (Ulysse)

Geirangerfjord, Nærøyfjord and other World Heritage fjords

Norway · Emission rule

In force

Tourist ships and ferries under 10,000 gross tonnes must be zero-emission in Norway's five World Heritage fjords; larger ships must comply from 2032.

Who pays
Cruise lines
From
1 January 2026 (under 10,000 GT); 1 January 2032 (larger ships)
Status
in force for small ships; announced for large ships

Sources

  • Introducing zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage Fjords (Government of Norway)

All Norwegian ports (municipal choice)

Norway · Fee

Proposed

The government proposes letting municipalities charge cruise passengers a flat fee per started 24 hours in port; the enabling visitor-contribution law took effect on 1 July 2026.

Amount
NOK 100 per passenger per started 24 hours
Who pays
Shipowner, operator and agent jointly liable (likely passed on to passengers)
From
Proposed from 1 January 2027
Status
proposed (consultation closed 22 June 2026)

Sources

  • Regjeringen foreslår cruiseavgift (Government of Norway, 20 Mar 2026)
  • 100 kroner per passenger: Norway reveals how new cruise tax will work (The Local Norway)

Oslo

Norway · Fee

Proposed

Oslo plans to use the new national rule to charge cruise passengers for each day a ship is in port.

Amount
Up to NOK 100 per passenger per day
Who pays
Passenger (via the cruise line)
From
2027, if approved
Status
proposed (needs city council approval)

Sources

  • Oslo planning new tax for cruise passengers (Cruise Industry News, Oct 2026)

Bergen

Norway · Visitor cap

In force

Bergen caps cruise traffic at four calls and 8,000 passengers a day and requires cruise ships to use shore power, aiming for all ships by 2026.

Amount
4 calls and 8,000 passengers per day
Who pays
Cruise lines
From
Cap in place since 2017–18; shore-power target 100% in 2026
Status
in force

Sources

  • More cruise tourists to Bergen in 2025 (Bergen Havn)

Svalbard protected areas

Norway · Visitor cap

In force

Passenger ships may carry no more than 200 passengers inside Svalbard's eastern and western protected areas, and landings are limited to 43 mapped sites.

Amount
200 passengers per ship
Who pays
Cruise lines
From
1 January 2025
Status
in force

All Icelandic ports

Iceland · Fee

In force

Cruise ships on international voyages pay an infrastructure fee for every passenger for each started 24 hours in Icelandic waters, whether or not passengers go ashore; it was cut for 2026.

Amount
ISK 1,600 per passenger per 24 hours (was ISK 2,500 in 2025)
Who pays
Cruise operator; usually charged to passengers' onboard accounts
From
1 January 2026 (reduced rate); fee introduced 1 January 2025
Status
in force

Portugal · Tax

In force

Questions

Do cruise passengers pay the Venice access fee?

Day visitors aged 14 and over pay on the set fee days if they enter the historic centre between 08:30 and 16:00. Passengers who only pass through the cruise terminal do not. See the Venice entry for amounts and dates.

Is there a cruise passenger fee in Greece?

Yes. Greece charges a per-passenger fee that is highest in Santorini and Mykonos in summer. The amounts by season are in the Greece entries.

Which cruise ports limit passenger numbers?

Several ports cap ships or passengers per day, including Dubrovnik, Bergen, Cannes, Juneau and Bar Harbor (July and August). Each cap and its status is listed on this page.

Are these fees included in my cruise fare?

It depends on the port and the cruise line. Where the source says who pays and how, the entry says so. If it does not, check with your cruise line.

What to Do in a 6-Hour Cruise Port Stop: The Port-by-Port Playbook

ElkePublished 2026-05-25Updated 2026-10-1612 min readUpdated for 2026 cruise season

Six hours on the schedule is not six hours in town

On a short call, three things eat into your time: getting off the ship, getting into town, and starting back early enough. How much each costs depends entirely on the port.

All examples below assume you are ashore at 09:00 with a 15:00 all-aboard. Each port's leave-by rule comes from our checked port guides (2026).

PortGetting inLeave-by ruleLeave by (15:00 all-aboard)Realistic time in town

The pattern is clear. Ports you can walk out of give you most of the day. Ports where the return depends on a train or a long queue give you very little.

Walk-off ports: Kotor and Naples

Kotor

The cruise quay is about 200 m from the Old Town's Sea Gate. Many ships anchor and tender to the same pier, which typically adds 30–60 minutes each way.

Kotor on 6 hours (docked, 15:00 all-aboard):

  • ·09:00 Walk through the Sea Gate
  • ·09:10 San Giovanni Fortress and the walls: €15, cash, 1.5–2 hours (2026). Start early; the upper two-thirds have no shade.
  • ·11:00 Cathedral of St Tryphon (€4, 30 minutes)
  • ·11:45 Maritime Museum of Montenegro (€4, 45 minutes; closed Sundays)
  • ·12:30 Lunch in the Old Town
  • ·14:00 Back at the gangway. If tendering, be at the tender pier by 13:30.

Cost: about €23 for the fortress, cathedral and museum. Skip: Perast (2.5–3 hours including travel) and the Ladder of Kotor (3–6 hours).

Naples

Ships dock at the Stazione Marittima, right in the city. Piazza del Plebiscito is 10–15 minutes on foot and Spaccanapoli about 15–20.

Naples on 6 hours:

  • ·09:00 Walk up Via Toledo to Spaccanapoli
  • ·09:20 Spaccanapoli and Via dei Tribunali, with San Gregorio Armeno (1.5–2 hours)
  • ·11:00 National Archaeological Museum (€20, about 2 hours; closed Tuesdays), or Cappella Sansevero (€12, booking required)
  • ·13:00 Pizza; the best-known pizzerias have queues at lunchtime, so eat early
  • ·13:45 Start walking back

Skip Pompeii. The rule is to be on a train back three hours before all-aboard, so 12:00. After the walk, the metro to Garibaldi and the 35-minute train, you would have about 1.5 hours at a site that needs three.

Short-transfer ports: Barcelona, Lisbon and Dubrovnik

Barcelona

Most ships dock at Moll Adossat, about 3 km out. The Cruise Bus (T3) takes about 10 minutes to the World Trade Center stop: €3.50 one way, €5 return, card only (2026).

Barcelona on 6 hours:

  • ·09:00 Cruise Bus into town
  • ·09:30 Metro L3 from Drassanes to Diagonal, then L5 to Sagrada Família (about 30 minutes)
  • ·10:00 Sagrada Família, timed ticket booked ahead (€26, about 1.5 hours)
  • ·11:45 Metro back towards the Gothic Quarter
  • ·12:15 Gothic Quarter walk, finishing near the sea
  • ·13:00 Lunch
  • ·13:45 At the Cruise Bus stop

Cost: about €37 for the Cruise Bus return, two metro singles and Sagrada Família. Choose one: Sagrada Família or Park Güell, not both. Park Güell adds a steep climb from the metro.

Lisbon

Most ships dock at Jardim do Tabaco, at the foot of Alfama. Praça do Comércio is a flat 14-minute walk.

Lisbon on 6 hours:

  • ·09:00 Walk up into Alfama
  • ·09:15 Castelo de São Jorge at opening (€17, 1 hour)
  • ·10:30 Alfama lanes and the miradouros (1–1.5 hours)
  • ·12:00 Down to the Baixa and Praça do Comércio; lunch a few streets back from Rua Augusta
  • ·13:30 Leave the Baixa for the terminal

Cost: €17 for the castle, plus transport if you use it: a €0.50 card and a €7.25 24-hour Carris/Metro ticket (2026). Skip: Sintra (allow 5–6 hours) and probably Belém. The rule from Belém is to leave 2 hours 15 minutes before all-aboard, and Jerónimos is closed on Mondays.

Dubrovnik

Most ships dock at Gruž, about 3 km from the Old Town. Libertas bus 1A or 1B reaches Pile Gate in 15–20 minutes for €2.50 on board (2026). In summer, buses fill near the port.

Dubrovnik on 6 hours:

  • ·09:00 Bus to Pile Gate
  • ·09:30 City walls (€40, 1.5–2 hours, 2026). One circuit, one entry.
  • ·11:30 Stradun and the Old Town, then lunch a street or two off Stradun
  • ·13:15 Leave Pile Gate

Cost: about €45 for the bus both ways and the walls. Skip: Lokrum (2.5–3 hours) and the cable car, unless you drop the walls.

Tender port: Santorini

All ships anchor. Independent passengers usually go after tour groups, so expect 30–60 minutes for an early tender on a busy day. From the Old Port, the cable car costs €10 one way (2025), with queues of 30–60 minutes or more; the alternative is about 560–600 steps.

On busy days, be at the top cable car station 2.5 hours before all-aboard. For 15:00, that is 12:30.

Santorini on 6 hours: Fira and the caldera path to Firostefani (15–20 minutes each way). Add Imerovigli only if the morning went smoothly: it adds another 20–30 minutes each way.

Skip Oia. It needs 2–3 hours including the bus, and the guide advises leaving Oia by 14:00 for a 17:30 all-aboard.

Cost: €20 for the cable car up and down (2025), or free on the steps.

Train ports: Rome, Athens and Florence

Rome (Civitavecchia)

The rule is to be on a train leaving Rome three hours before all-aboard. For 15:00, that is 12:00. The journey in takes the shuttle, a 15–20 minute walk and 50–60 minutes on the FL5 to San Pietro, with two to three trains an hour. You would reach Rome at around 10:30 at best, leaving about an hour.

Verdict: Not worth it on a 6-hour call. Check whether your call is really that short. If it is, stay in Civitavecchia: Forte Michelangelo is on the walk to the station.

Athens (Piraeus)

The metro is short, about 20 minutes, but the walk to it is 15 minutes from Terminal A and about 30 from Terminals B and C. The rule is to be on a metro back by 2 hours 45 minutes before all-aboard from Terminal A, 3 hours from B and C. That gives roughly 2–2.5 hours in central Athens.

Do: The Acropolis only (about 2 hours, €30 with a timed slot, 2026), booked for an early slot. Monastiraki to the entrance is 10–15 minutes uphill. Skip: Everything else. Check for metro strikes the evening before.

Florence (from Livorno)

The rule is to be on a train out of Santa Maria Novella 3.5 hours before all-aboard: 11:30 for a 15:00 all-aboard. After the shuttle, the bus and a 70–90 minute train, you would barely arrive.

Verdict: Not possible. Pisa is closer: the train takes 15–20 minutes and the rule is to be on a train back two hours before all-aboard. Or stay in Livorno.

A framework for any 6-hour call

  1. ·Find the port's leave-by rule and work back from all-aboard.
  2. ·Subtract the journey in. What remains is your window.
  3. ·Choose one main thing, plus lunch if there is time.
  4. ·Book the main sight ahead if it uses timed tickets.
  5. ·Set an alarm for the leave-by time. When it goes off, you leave.

Frequently asked questions

How much time do I actually get on a 6-hour port call? At walk-off ports such as Kotor and Naples, about 4–4.5 hours. At short-transfer ports such as Barcelona, Lisbon and Dubrovnik, about 3.5–4 hours. In Santorini, about 1.5–2 hours in Fira. Rome and Florence are not realistic.

Is 6 hours enough to visit Pompeii from Naples? No. You need to be on a train back three hours before all-aboard, which leaves about 1.5 hours at a site that needs three.

Is 6 hours enough to visit Rome from Civitavecchia? No. With the rule of a train out of Rome three hours before all-aboard, you get about an hour in the city.

Which port works best on 6 hours? Kotor, if your ship docks: the quay is about 200 m from the Sea Gate, and the fortress, the Old Town and lunch all fit.

Should I book a ship excursion on a 6-hour call? Consider it where the return depends on a train, or on a strike day. If the ship's own coach is late, the ship waits. At walk-off ports such as Kotor, Valletta or Naples, independent planning is manageable.

The Mediterranean is the world's most popular cruise region — and for good reason. In a single week at sea, passengers move between ancient Roman cities, Greek island caldera views, medieval Croatian fortifications, and Portuguese coastal beauty. But not all Mediterranean cruise ports are equal from the perspective of an independent traveller with 6–8 hours ashore. Some ports reward careful planners with extraordinary days. Others punish lack of preparation with expensive taxis, long queues, and a rushed lunch somewhere you shouldn't have eaten. This ranking takes a different approach to the usual "best ports" lists: it ranks entirely on what you can actually achieve independently, in the time you have, with real logistics and real costs.

How we ranked these Mediterranean cruise ports

This list is built on five specific criteria that matter for independent cruise port visitors, not just general travel appeal. First: terminal-to-city transport — how easy, fast, and affordable is the journey from gangway to the heart of the experience? Second: site density and compactness — how much can you accomplish within walking distance once you've arrived, without needing multiple secondary journeys? Third: independent accessability — are the best experiences freely accessible without a guide, or do they require group access or specialist logistics? Fourth: cost efficiency versus ship excursion pricing — how much can you save by planning independently, and is the saving worth the effort? Fifth: forgiveness for timing errors — how badly does a late start or a slow afternoon actually hurt you, and how recoverable is the port from a timing mistake?

The result is a ranking that rewards ports which work exceptionally well for independent travellers — not necessarily the most famous or photographed destinations, but the ones where a well-planned day consistently produces an extraordinary result. You'll notice that compactness ranks extremely highly. A UNESCO World Heritage Site you can walk to from the gangway scores above a more spectacular destination requiring a 90-minute transfer each way.

1. Dubrovnik, Croatia — The benchmark Mediterranean cruise port day

Dubrovnik is the closest thing to a perfect cruise port that the Mediterranean offers. The Old Town — a medieval fortified city of extraordinary preservation — is accessible from the cruise terminal by a two-euro bus ride in 15 minutes. Once through Pile Gate, every significant experience is within 20 minutes on foot.

The City Walls (€35, open from 08:00) are the centrepiece: a 2km circuit of medieval fortifications with extraordinary views across the orange-red rooftops and the Adriatic beyond. Walk them before 09:30 and you'll share them with perhaps 50 other people. Arrive at 11:00 and you'll share them with several thousand. The difference is not subtle.

Beyond the walls: the Stradun limestone boulevard, the Rector's Palace (€13), the Franciscan Monastery with one of Europe's oldest pharmacies, the backstreet network that most excursion passengers never find. A konoba lunch in the streets behind the Stradun costs €15–20 per person and is significantly better than anything on the tourist drag. The Srđ Hill cable car (€30 return) is optional but spectacular.

The main challenge is Dubrovnik's enormous popularity in July and August. Managing crowds through timing — arriving early, walking the walls before 09:30, and being back at the terminal by 15:30 — is the single biggest lever available to any independent visitor.

Total cost for an exceptional Dubrovnik day: €37–89 per person (City Walls + bus + lunch ± cable car). Ship excursion equivalent: €89–115 per person. Saving: €52–76 per person.

2. Kotor, Montenegro — The best walk-off cruise port in the Adriatic

Kotor ranks second because it solves the terminal-to-experience problem completely. You walk 200 metres from the gangway through the Sea Gate, and you're inside a UNESCO World Heritage medieval walled city. There is no taxi queue, no bus research, no 25-minute transfer, no ticking meter. Every minute ashore is spent in quality.

The St John Fortress hike (€8, approximately 1,350 steps to 260 metres above the bay) is the highest-priority experience. The view from the top — the Bay of Kotor, the cruise ships miniaturised below, the surrounding mountains — is one of the finest in the Mediterranean. Allow 60–90 minutes for the round trip. Do it first, before 10:00, before the heat builds.

The Old Town itself covers about 500 metres at its widest. The Cathedral of Saint Tryphon (€3), the Maritime Museum (€5), and Trg od Oružja square are all worth visiting, but the real pleasure of Kotor is unhurried wandering through the medieval lanes. Kotor's famous cats add an unexpected charm to every corner.

A konoba lunch of fresh Adriatic fish, black risotto, and local Vranac wine costs €12–18 per person. The restaurants on the main square overcharge. The places one street back are significantly better at half the price.

Total cost for a perfect Kotor day: €23–35 per person. Ship excursion equivalent: €65–89. This is among the highest value-for-cost ratios of any Mediterranean cruise port.

3. Barcelona, Spain — Maximum reward per hour in Europe

Barcelona is a more complex proposition than Kotor or Dubrovnik because the terminal is 3–5km from the city centre — a €12–15 Uber or taxi journey that takes 20–30 minutes. Once you're in central Barcelona, however, the experience-per-hour ratio is exceptional. Few cities pack this much world-class culture into a compact, navigable area.

The Gothic Quarter and La Boqueria market are within 10 minutes walk of each other. The Sagrada Família (advance tickets essential at €26–36) is three metro stops from Las Ramblas on Line 3. Barceloneta Beach is 20 minutes walk from the old town. The Picasso Museum (€16) is a 15-minute walk from the Gothic Quarter.

The strategic mistake most Barcelona port day visitors make is ambition: trying to do Gaudí, beach, Gothic Quarter, market, and tapas in a single day. Choose two or three experiences and do them properly, with time to eat a genuine lunch somewhere off the tourist trail at 13:00 rather than a rushed panini at 14:30.

A well-planned Barcelona day costs approximately €50–75 per person including terminal transport, Sagrada Família entry, and a proper sit-down lunch. Ship excursion equivalent: €119 per person. The DIY experience is objectively better and costs significantly less.

4. Santorini, Greece — Spectacular but demanding, and only for the prepared

Santorini belongs in the top five of any Mediterranean cruise port ranking for one simple reason: the caldera views from Fira and Oia are genuinely extraordinary in a way that photographs fail to capture. The deep blue of the submerged volcanic caldera, the white cubic architecture, the quality of the Aegean light — it's as good as its reputation.

The complexity is real, and it changes the entire calculation compared to a walk-off port. Santorini is a tender port: your ship anchors in the caldera and you transfer to shore on small boats. The tender process adds 20–35 minutes each way to your day. Return tender queues on busy summer days (July–August) with multiple ships in the caldera regularly run 45–75 minutes — this must be factored into your return timing.

The rule for Santorini: apply the 120-minute buffer, not 90. Be at the tender dock by 15:00 if your all-aboard is 17:00. Plan for 4–5 effective hours ashore, not 7.

The trade-off is worth making if you go in with clear expectations. Santorini on its own terms — understood as a 4-hour window for the most spectacular views in the Mediterranean, with precise timing — is extraordinary. Santorini misunderstood as an all-day casual exploration is the source of more near-misses and actual missed ships than any other Mediterranean port.

5–12: The rest of the Mediterranean ranking

5. Lisbon, Portugal — The most underrated major city port in Western Europe. The Santa Apolónia terminal puts you 20 minutes walk from Alfama, one of the most beautiful living historic districts in Europe. Belém by taxi takes 15 minutes and contains the Jerónimos Monastery (UNESCO, €10) and the original Pastéis de Belém. An extraordinary day costs under €50 per person.

6. Naples, Italy — The most criminally underrated cruise destination in the Mediterranean. The terminal is walkable to Spaccanapoli, the city's extraordinary main artery. World-class pizza at Sorbillo or Da Michele for €8. The National Archaeological Museum contains the finest collection of Roman artefacts in existence. Naples as a destination is exceptional; Naples as a gateway to Pompeii is the conventional choice.

7. Athens (Piraeus), Greece — The most logistically challenging major port (50-minute metro journey) but containing the Acropolis, one of the genuine wonders of the world. Focus on one zone of Athens, pre-book everything, and the reward is proportionate.

8. Rome (Civitavecchia), Italy — 75km from Rome means a 75-minute train journey each way. You have approximately 6 hours in the city on a 10-hour port day. Choose one zone of Rome and do it properly.

9. Palma de Mallorca, Spain — An excellent Old Town, a magnificent Gothic cathedral (La Seu, €9), and a central terminal that puts you walking distance from everything. Often overlooked on Western Mediterranean itineraries.

10. Valletta, Malta — Europe's smallest capital, almost entirely walkable from the cruise terminal, and extraordinarily dense with history. One of the most forgiving ports for first-time independent travellers.

11. Split, Croatia — Diocletian's Palace, where 3,000 people still live inside a Roman emperor's retirement complex. Walk-off access from the terminal. Significantly less crowded than Dubrovnik.

12. Istanbul, Turkey — Unparalleled reward, complex logistics. The most intellectually extraordinary cruise port in the world, but requires genuine planning.
